title: The Greatness of Christ's Glory and True Splendor
english: Glory is small for men of little thought and little goodness. Thus, physicians who bring health to those who are well seem to take glory for themselves—it has been thought rather that the healthy person is more glorious than the one suffering—but the glory is not great. Similarly for a pilot.

In the salvation of God, therefore, there is 'great glory'; for this salvation touches the mind and the soul. And of all that is in us, the mind differs and the soul from the body, even if it does not seem so to others. And it is possible even to call the Savior himself 'salvation', as he is found in many places: 'All the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our God' (Ps 95:3). 'And all flesh shall see the salvation of God' (Isa 49:6), instead of 'every man' or 'every sensitive soul'. In this salvation, therefore, is 'great glory'.

Even if the death which he received seems to be without honor—for 'cursed is everyone hanging on a tree' (Gal 3:13) according to the law—yet this seeming dishonor was able to receive such glory from the purpose of salvation, because salvation has become not of food, nor of men simply, but of soul and mind and spirit, as Paul writes: 'Your whole spirit and soul and body' (1 Thess 5:23). The seeming dishonor is therefore a glory surpassing all.

I wish to remind you of a thought. When I was speaking concerning the Gospel, concerning that place: 'He who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do, and greater than these he will do' (John 14:12), to others this interpretation was also given: if you consider the analogy of the one doing, the great things are small; as they are small compared to God. For the apostles did not perform sensible works greater than those of the Savior. The Savior raised Lazarus, already on the fourth day being in death and near to decomposing and already having reached the point of stinking. The apostles did not do anything of this kind. Jesus brought the blind from birth to sight. If, however, you consider these works of the Savior, they are small compared to having performed the rational essence, the heavens, the souls. And the works of the apostles, even if they were greater than those of the Savior, since their power is [from Him], are rather called greater than those which the Savior did; for they were not able to do greater than these. But Jesus both did and always does. And the apostle says: 'We see the one being humbled'...

Jesus [was humbled] through the suffering of death. He was humbled through the suffering of death, but he was crowned with "glory and honor." The humbling led to glory, and indeed it led to the greatest. I reason that "the sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that is about to be revealed" (Rom 8:18). And those sufferings of Christ are those which his imitators suffer, having first suffered as he did. Great, therefore, is his glory. Even if it be a cross, even if it be death, if you see the goal of salvation and the Savior, what greatness is there? Not great is the glory of others. For indeed there are times when they had glory, and yet the glory departed even while they were living.

Thus also I have heard what is said in Isaiah: "and of his peace there is no limit" (Isa 9:7). "Justice and an abundance of peace rise in his days until the moon is taken away." Observe the peace that they caused to rise; for it holds until the completion, for nothing else signifies the taking away of the moon except the completion, when "the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light" (Matt 24:29). Peace is not in one nation, nor on earth alone; for he "made peace" through "the blood of his cross" (Eph 2:14), not only "the things on earth," but also "the things in the heavens."

6 Glory and splendor shall be laid upon him. Glory and splendor are laid upon him along with this great glory which exists in his salvation. And splendor consists of things and endeavors in which there is what is becoming. Works done from virtue become fittingly. Many things seem to men to be becoming, but they are not truly becoming; just as I have said concerning glory, that there are honors and dignities which are not such things as men think them to be, but they were supposed by them to be such. Splendor, therefore, they call—take the meaning from the literal sense, from history—such as are gladiators, and if they are small-spoken, they diminish the contests and the expenses from a small intention, and they seem to do what is becoming for the athlete, but they do it little, and they are called these "small-splendid" ones; for they are not found to be surpassing, being less than nothing in the becoming, compared to the gladiators before them. This, therefore, is called splendor, when in...

title: True Magnificence vs. Vanity
english: Let there be a size that is appropriate. But it is most especially magnificence when it is for the sake of the appropriate itself, and not for the sake of anything else.

Let it be said: if one, being rich, spends great things on small matters and small celebrations, he is not magnificent. It is an excess of magnificence, just as we say that rashness is an excess of courage and impiety is an excess of piety. For example, if someone provides a feast for his drinking companions and spends as much as no one else spends at weddings, he is not magnificent. It happens for the sake of vainglory. But magnificence does not happen for the sake of vainglory.

Let us come from being led by the sensible things to the things about which the word is: the Savior worked the appropriate in great things. And the righteous man shows the appropriate in great things toward men. What is greater than saving the inhabited world, and making peace not only of the earthly things, but also of the heavenly things? What is greater than rectifying that by which the heavenly, the earthly, and the subterranean things bend the knee to the Savior for the glory of God the Father? This glory is magnificence, and it has a kinship with propriety. And concerning Him, the God, it is said: 'The Lord has reigned, He has put on propriety' (Ps 96:10). This propriety and magnificence are the same.

To whom did it befit to save the men, or he who did not have sin? He did not have sin, knowing that it is beautiful to abstain from sin, to have righteousness, that it is beautiful to not retaliate against one who insults, and not to defend those who behave wickedly. 'The one suffering,' He says, 'did not threaten' (Ps 21:1). Not only did He not do what was deserved, but He did not even threaten. A threat is a prior announcement of fearful things. But when it is no longer a prior announcement, but happens by the outcome, it is no longer a threat.

'Glory and magnificence You will lay upon him' (Ps 103:2). And it is good also to say 'You will lay upon.' In another text, this is also attributed to Him: for not only now when He arrived, did He begin to place this glory and this magnificence in the rational [things], but always and everywhere, as He was able, He did this. And the glory and magnificence through His arrival have become an addition, such as through the cross. For 'You will give him a blessing unto the age of ages' (Ps 21:7). Thus, as we have said concerning life: not so that He himself...
unto the age of ages

title: The Nature of Hope and Scientific Expectation
english: "of the Most High". See: it seems here to have been sent from the Father and the Holy Spirit. Others, however, read it this way, and this reading is better: "and the Lord, the Lord, has sent me; and his Spirit also has sent" (Ps 2:7); the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. The former version says this: that the Father and the Holy Spirit sent the Son. Each person receives the reading according to his own appropriate understanding, as has already been said. And here, therefore, there is a person of the Lord being spoken of here. And the Son is his image, "the character of his substance."

Concerning the one having taken on a face by the Savior and every righteous man, it is said: "rejoice him in joy with your face" (Ps 2:11), for when the Son and the Father come, and someone has seen the character immediately and the one of whom the character is: "he who has seen me has seen the Father" (Ps 2:12). Rejoicing happens by God and of his own face. And it is also possible to take it this way: "rejoice him in joy with your face." Therefore, this is said concerning every righteous man: for your face, through which "in image and likeness" (Gen 1:26) it has become, shall be revealed of him.

And I say: things that have happened, even if they are separate, often exist together with substances; for example, color: for the body is not first created, and then it is colored; it is created having been colored, and nevertheless we say that color is in certain things among those things that happen and un-happen. I added "in certain things," since among sensible things, it neither comes upon nor goes away from the snow; nor does moisture come upon or go away from water; for it is essential. Since, therefore, the rational is good from the beginning, it is not good in the same way as God; for it is not good according to substance, but according to a state and a disposition. Even if man has become "in image and likeness" (Gen 1:26), this thing which has form is separate, being cast off and being taken up. However, when God saves, every image will be destroyed. But this shall be revealed in the one having been saved.
For the king hopes in the Lord (Ps 20:7). This king hopes in the Lord. He hopes that there will be salvation for those for whom he has come to suffer. The end of the one striving is not in doubt.

But he hopes unchangeably; for 'in the mercy of the Most High he is not shaken' (Ps 56:3). Therefore his hope does not fall. And I offer a paradigm, though it is perhaps a violent one: no one hopes for things present. The healthy man does not hope to be healthy, nor the rich man to be rich. It is of things to come. Hope and expectation are the same. Expectation is a genus of hope; for hope is indeed the expectation of good things from God.

Of things to come, the former [the possible] has an existence such that it is able to happen or not to happen as it may turn out, but the latter [the certain] will certainly happen; for example, what I say scientifically, by way of an image: that after such a period there is an eclipse of the sun. Only the expert hopes for this; for the other person does not know at all whether it happens or does not happen. It is good to remind of this that there are four problems: two simple and two compound. Simple are 'that it is' and 'what it is.' Then compound are 'how it is' and 'why it is.'

It is therefore for the expert to expect these things which will certainly happen scientifically. For he knows both that an eclipse is, and what an eclipse is, namely a running-to-meet of the moon. And how it happens: that, when the moon becomes in opposition under the sun, an eclipse happens. Behold, the 'how it happens.' And the 'why it is so': because the sun, revolving, moves in varying intervals. And under the solar circle is that of the moon. Therefore it does not always happen in opposition. It is as if there are two circles. If it happens thus and again into the lower [one], the lower thing happening hides the upper. They say, therefore, that an eclipse is the opposition of the moon toward the sun.

It is therefore for the expert to know this unpassable expectation. And of things happening by chance, let them expect, I say, rain or good fortune. But many dispute these things. He says, therefore: 'Rejoice in him with joy; for the king hopes in the Lord' (Ps 21:14). The king is the one hoping. And his hope and expectation are unpassable. And he says: 'In the mercy of the Most High he shall not be shaken' (Ps 56:3). He being shown mercy by the Most High is not shaken; for then he is shaken, when the subjects are found unworthy of his kingship. And he abandons them, he turns away from them. And to hope is as to be persuaded by God, in this way.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
